action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.label: Cardiac MIBG scintigraphy for early severe orthostatic hypotension with parkinsonism
action_criteria.rationale: Early severe autonomic failure is an MDS red flag that raises MSA; cardiac sympathetic denervation on MIBG is an MDS supportive criterion for PD and is usually absent in MSA, so the result decides whether the red flag is counterbalanced [Postuma_2015]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not prescribe domperidone for levodopa-related nausea while he takes flecainide (additive QT prolongation)
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a patient with cognitive impairment
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015): right-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, rigidity and a right-hand rest tremor; one red flag (severe orthostatic hypotension, 42/30 mmHg at 3 minutes, within 5 years of onset) counterbalanced by two supportive criteria (rest tremor, and cardiac sympathetic denervation on MIBG); anosmia on the UPSIT (14/40, when tested) further favours PD over MSA, in which smell is usually preserved, but the post-viral history is a competing cause, so the MIBG carries the second supportive criterion and the red flag keeps the diagnosis clinically probable [Postuma_2015]

Treat the orthostatic hypotension: review metoprolol with his cardiologist, advise 2 to 2.5 L of fluid a day, small meals (post-prandial symptoms), slow staged rising, head-up tilt of the bed and abdominal compression; if symptoms persist, consider midodrine or fludrocortisone with supine blood pressure and potassium monitoring

Start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), review the response after 2 to 3 months, and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each step; prefer levodopa to a dopamine agonist, which worsens orthostatic hypotension, and if an agonist is used warn about impulse control disorders and excessive daytime sleepiness [NICE_NG71]

Advise bedroom safety for the injurious dream enactment (protect his wife, pad the bedside, remove sharp objects) and review clonazepam, which adds sedation and fall risk with orthostatic hypotension; melatonin is an alternative
Refer to physiotherapy for balance and fall prevention after his fall and two near-falls

The near-syncope occurs on standing with a measured orthostatic fall, and his arrhythmia is followed by cardiology: an echocardiogram does not inform the parkinsonism

key_clinical_evidence: Right-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and a 4-5 Hz right-hand rest tremor: parkinsonism with one supportive criterion on examination [Postuma_2015]
Orthostatic fall of 36/26 mmHg at 1 minute and 42/30 mmHg at 3 minutes within 2 years of onset: severe autonomic failure, one MDS red flag; metoprolol makes the heart-rate response uninterpretable
Reduced cardiac MIBG uptake (delayed H/M 1.21, washout 38%): cardiac sympathetic denervation, the second supportive criterion, counterbalancing the red flag [Postuma_2015]
MRI without putaminal, pontine or cerebellar abnormality; bilateral nigrosome-1 loss on SWI [Schwarz_2014]

Clinically diagnosed REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation and smell loss preceding the motor signs: prodromal synucleinopathy features; anosmia on a validated test (UPSIT 14/40) has a competing post-viral explanation, so the MIBG carries the second supportive criterion [Berg_2015]
Father and brother with essential tremor led to an initial ET label that the rest tremor, decrement and rigidity do not fit

contraindications: Domperidone is not advised with flecainide: both prolong the QT interval.
Non-selective MAO inhibitors with levodopa: risk of hypertensive crisis.
interactions: Metoprolol lowers standing blood pressure and blunts the compensatory heart-rate rise, adding to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need and dose with cardiology and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Sertraline with an MAO-B inhibitor: serotonin syndrome is rare; use the lowest dose and monitor. Fluoxetine and fluvoxamine are best avoided with rasagiline.
Clonazepam adds sedation and fall risk with dopaminergic drugs in older patients.
warnings: Midodrine can be considered for symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; it raises supine blood pressure (measure it lying, avoid doses within 4 hours of bedtime) and can cause reflex bradycardia, additive to metoprolol.
Fludrocortisone causes fluid retention, hypokalaemia and supine hypertension; hypokalaemia increases the proarrhythmic risk of flecainide.
Flecainide, apixaban and polyethylene glycol 3350: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Takeshi Yamamoto is a 63-year-old right-handed retired dentist who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic with his wife for evaluation of progressive motor slowing, gait instability, and recurrent near-falls that have developed insidiously over the past two years. His wife first noticed changes approximately two years ago when he began having difficulty performing fine dental procedures, particularly precision work requiring steady hands. He attributed this initially to fatigue and age-related changes, but the difficulties progressed to the point where he elected to retire from his practice one year ago. Over the same period, his wife observed that his movements became slower and more effortful, particularly with his right hand, affecting routine activities such as buttoning his shirt, managing chopsticks at meals, and getting in and out of the car. She describes his facial expression as increasingly blank, noting that friends have commented he appears depressed or disinterested even when engaged in conversation. His handwriting has become progressively smaller to the point of illegibility on prescription pads in the final months of his practice. Approximately eighteen months ago, he experienced his first significant balance event when he stumbled backward off a step in his garden and fell, sustaining a bruised elbow. Since then, he has had two near-falls, both when light-headed after standing up, without a further fall. He has become more cautious and avoids stairs when possible. Over the past year his wife has also noticed a tremor of his right hand when it rests in his lap. Concurrently, he has developed progressively worsening lightheadedness upon standing, particularly in the morning and after meals. On two occasions in the past six months, he has experienced near-syncope requiring him to sit down immediately. His cardiologist attributed this to his cardiac medications, but dose adjustments to his metoprolol have not resolved the symptoms; he remains on metoprolol, which limits his heart-rate response on standing. His chronic constipation, which began approximately three years ago, has worsened considerably despite daily polyethylene glycol, and he frequently goes four to five days without a bowel movement. He denies urinary urgency, incontinence or difficulty emptying his bladder. His wife reports that approximately two years ago he began acting out vivid dreams, including shouting, punching, and kicking during sleep, sometimes injuring her; this was diagnosed as REM sleep behavior disorder and treated with low-dose clonazepam with partial improvement. He lost his sense of smell approximately four years ago following a severe upper respiratory infection, though his wife notes it never returned and questions whether this predated the infection. He denies visual hallucinations. He has noticed mild difficulties with concentration and multitasking over the past year but denies significant memory loss. Importantly, his family history is notable for essential tremor in his father and one brother, which initially led his primary care physician to suspect familial essential tremor as the cause of his motor difficulties. He has not been exposed to neuroleptics, metoclopramide, or other dopamine-blocking agents. He has no history of encephalitis, significant head trauma, or toxic exposures including manganese or carbon monoxide.

neurological_exam.additional: Orthostatic vital signs: supine BP 138/84 mmHg, HR 64; standing at 1 minute BP 102/58 mmHg, HR 68 (drop of 36/26 mmHg). Standing at 3 minutes BP 96/54 mmHg, HR 70. Patient reports lightheadedness and visual graying upon standing. Glabellar tap: persistent (Myerson sign positive). No alien limb phenomenon. No apraxia of eyelid opening. No applause sign. Seborrheic dermatitis noted on forehead and nasolabial folds.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements slow, more on the right, without cerebellar-type irregularity or intention tremor.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements full. No vertical gaze palsy; vertical saccades of normal speed. Smooth pursuit mildly saccadic. Reduced blink rate noted. Facial expression markedly hypomimic bilaterally. Hearing intact to finger rub. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Anosmia confirmed on bedside testing with coffee grounds and peppermint.
neurological_exam.gait: Narrow-based, with markedly reduced right arm swing and mildly reduced left arm swing. Stride length shortened with a mild shuffling quality. Turns require 4-5 steps. Pull test: three steps backward with unaided recovery. No freezing. Tandem gait performed with mild unsteadiness. No festination.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, date, and situation. MMSE 27/30 (lost 1 point on serial sevens, 1 point on delayed recall, 1 point on pentagons). MoCA 23/30, losing one point each on trail-making, clock drawing, serial subtraction and letter fluency, and three on delayed recall. Speech is mildly hypophonic with occasional word-finding pauses. Affect is blunted. No hallucinations reported.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal. Cogwheel rigidity at both wrists and elbows, more marked on the right; mild rigidity in the right leg. Bradykinesia with progressive decrement in amplitude and hesitation on finger tapping, hand movements and pronation-supination, clearly worse on the right. Rest tremor of the right hand at 4-5 Hz, re-emerging after a latency when the arms are held outstretched; mild postural tremor of both hands. No dystonia or myoclonus observed.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, and patellar bilaterally. Achilles reflexes 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No palmomental or grasp reflexes.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally. Vibration sense mildly diminished at ankles. Romberg negative.
